q: The lesson "His First Flight" is about which young bird?
o: A crow
A young seagull
A pigeon
An eagle
e: Liam O'Flaherty's story "His First Flight" is about a young seagull overcoming his fear to fly for the first time.

q: Who is the author of "His First Flight"?
o: Liam O'Flaherty
Frederick Forsyth
G.L. Fuentes
Carolyn Wells
e: Liam O'Flaherty wrote "His First Flight", whereas Frederick Forsyth wrote "The Black Aeroplane".

q: Why was the young seagull afraid to fly?
o: Because his wings were broken
Because he was afraid of the dark
Because his parents forbade him from flying
Because he saw the vast expanse of sea beneath and felt certain his wings would never support him
e: Seeing the great expanse of sea stretching miles down beneath the ledge, he felt certain his wings would never support him.

q: For how long had the young seagull been left alone on the ledge before his first flight?
o: Twelve hours
One week
Twenty-four hours
Three days
e: The text states: "That was twenty-four hours ago. Since then nobody had come near him."

q: What finally urged the young seagull to make his first flight?
o: A strong gust of wind
The sight of a piece of fish in his mother's beak—maddened by hunger, he dived at it
A push from his older brother
Fear of a predator
e: Maddened by hunger, he dived at the piece of fish held in his mother's beak and plunged outward into space, beginning his first flight.

q: Which fish had the young seagull's older brother caught for the first time?
o: Herring
Dog-fish
Salmon
Shark
e: He saw his older brother catch his first herring; at the end of the story, the family offered the young seagull scraps of dog-fish.

q: In which direction did the young seagull's ledge face under the blazing sun?
o: North
West
East
South
e: The text states: "The sun was now ascending the sky, blazing on his ledge that faced the south."

q: When the young seagull dropped his legs onto the green sea at the end, what happened?
o: He sank completely underwater
He flew straight back to the ledge
His legs sank in, then his belly touched it and he floated smoothly on it
A shark chased him away
e: His feet sank into the sea, then his belly touched it and he sank no farther—he was floating safely while his family praised him.

q: Who is the author of the story "The Black Aeroplane"?
o: Liam O'Flaherty
Frederick Forsyth
Anton Chekhov
Ruskin Bond
e: Frederick Forsyth wrote "The Black Aeroplane", the second part of "Two Stories about Flying".

q: What was the name of the aeroplane that the narrator was flying in "The Black Aeroplane"?
o: Old Dakota (DS 088)
Boeing 747
Airbus A320
Concorde
e: The narrator was flying his old Dakota aeroplane, call sign DS 088.

q: Where was the pilot flying from and to in "The Black Aeroplane"?
o: From England to France
From Germany to Paris
From France to New York
Over France back to England
e: The story begins: "I was flying my old Dakota aeroplane over France back to England."

q: What direction did Paris Control instruct the Dakota pilot to turn?
o: Twelve degrees east
Fifteen degrees north
Twelve degrees west
Ten degrees south
e: Paris Control instructed: "You ought to turn twelve degrees west now, DS 088. Over."

q: How far was the pilot from Paris when he saw the huge black storm clouds?
o: 50 kilometres
150 kilometres
500 kilometres
20 kilometres
e: "Paris was about 150 kilometres behind me when I saw the clouds. Storm clouds. They were huge."

q: Why did the pilot take the risk of flying straight into the storm instead of going back to Paris?
o: Because he wanted to get home to his family in time for a good big English breakfast
To win an aviation award
Because Paris airport had closed down
Because another pilot challenged him
e: Longing for his holiday and a "good big English breakfast" with his family, he decided, "I'll take the risk" and flew straight into the storm.

q: What was unusual about the appearance of the mysterious black aeroplane in the storm?
o: It was painted bright red
It was parked on the runway
It had four giant jet engines
It had no lights on its wings
e: The narrator explicitly notes: "It had no lights on its wings, but I could see it flying next to me through the storm."

q: What did the woman at the control centre tell the narrator when he asked about the other pilot?
o: That the other pilot had just stepped out for tea
That it was a secret military jet
That no other aeroplanes were flying that night; only his plane appeared on the radar
That the other plane crashed
e: She laughed strangely and said: "No other aeroplanes were flying tonight. Yours was the only one I could see on the radar."

q: Who composed the humorous poem "How to Tell Wild Animals"?
o: Robin Klein
Carolyn Wells
Adrienne Rich
John Berryman
e: Carolyn Wells wrote "How to Tell Wild Animals", while John Berryman wrote "The Ball Poem".

q: According to "How to Tell Wild Animals", which creature identifies itself by hugging you very, very hard?
o: Bear
Bengal Tiger
Leopard
Crocodile
e: Stanza 4 humorously warns that a creature in your yard who "hugs you very, very hard" is definitely a Bear.

q: How does Carolyn Wells distinguish between a Hyena and a Crocodile in "How to Tell Wild Animals"?
o: Hyenas are tiny and crocodiles can fly
Hyenas have black stripes on yellow
Crocodiles climb trees while hyenas swim
Hyenas come with merry smiles, whereas if they weep they are crocodiles
e: The poem states: "Hyenas come with merry smiles; / But if they weep they're Crocodiles."

q: Which features of a true Chameleon are described in "How to Tell Wild Animals"?
o: It is large and tawny
It hugs tightly
It is small like a lizard, has no ears or wings, and blends into the tree so you see "nothing on the tree"
It has black stripes on yellow ground
e: A true chameleon is small, lizard-like, has no ears or wings, and camouflages so well that "If there is nothing on the tree, / 'Tis the chameleon you see."

q: Which wild animal is recognized by "black stripes on a yellow ground"?
o: Asian Lion
Bengal Tiger
Leopard
Hyena
e: Stanza 2 identifies the "noble wild beast" with "black stripes on a yellow ground" as the Bengal Tiger (unlike the spotted leopard).

q: Where is the Asian Lion found and what colour is it according to Carolyn Wells?
o: Jungles in the east; large and tawny (brownish-yellow)
Western forests; pure white
Northern icy peaks; black
Coral islands; blue
e: The opening stanza places the "large and tawny beast" in the "jungles in the east".

q: Who is the poet of "The Ball Poem"?
o: Robert Frost
Carolyn Wells
Leslie Norris
John Berryman
e: John Berryman composed "The Ball Poem".

q: What has the boy lost in "The Ball Poem"?
o: His book
His toy car
His ball
His wallet
e: The opening line states: "What is the boy now, who has lost his ball."

q: Where does the boy's ball finally go after bouncing down the street?
o: Into a dense forest
Into the water of the harbour
Into a deep dry well
Onto a school roof
e: The ball bounces merrily down the street and drops straight into the water of the harbour.

q: According to "The Ball Poem", how much would another ball cost that the poet calls "worthless"?
o: A dime (10 cents)
One dollar
A hundred pesos
Ten pounds
e: The poet says "A dime, another ball, is worthless"—where a dime equals 10 U.S. cents.

q: How does the boy react immediately after losing his ball into the water?
o: He laughs and runs back home
He quarrels with the poet
He immediately buys a new ball
An ultimate shaking grief fixes him as he stands rigid, trembling, and staring down
e: The poem depicts him struck by "an ultimate shaking grief", standing rigid and trembling as he stares into the harbour.

q: Why does the poet decide NOT to intrude on the grieving boy in "The Ball Poem"?
o: Because he is annoyed with the boy
Because the poet had no money at all
Because the boy must learn his first responsibility and the nature of loss on his own
Because he was rushing to catch a train
e: No external coin can replace lost memories; the boy must independently learn responsibility and "how to stand up" after loss.

q: What does the word "epistemology" refer to in "The epistemology of loss"?
o: A rulebook of sports
The study/understanding of the nature of knowledge—here, understanding what loss truly means
Oceanography
Currency exchange rate
e: Derived from Greek "episteme" (knowledge), "epistemology of loss" means understanding the nature and meaning of loss in human life.

q: What is the rhyme scheme or verse form of "The Ball Poem"?
o: Free verse (no fixed rhyme scheme)
Rhyming quatrains (abab)
Shakespearean sonnet
Couplets (aabb)
e: John Berryman wrote "The Ball Poem" in unrhymed free verse without a regular rhyme scheme.

q: How did the young seagull's parents threaten him when he refused to fly from the ledge?
o: Threatening to let him starve on his ledge unless he flew away
They would leave him on another island
They would break his nest
They would call fishermen
e: His father and mother came around calling shrilly, upbraiding him, and "threatening to let him starve on his ledge unless he flew away."

q: What trick did the young seagull try on the brink of the ledge to draw his family's attention?
o: He hid inside his hole permanently
He clapped his wings loudly
He threw pebbles into the sea
He stood on one leg with the other hidden under his wing, closed his eyes one by one, and pretended to be falling asleep
e: He stood on one leg with the other tucked under his wing, closed one eye then the other, and "pretended to be falling asleep", yet they took no notice.

q: While the mother looked at the young seagull, what was his father doing on the plateau?
o: Fast asleep next to the brothers
Diving for herrings
Preening the feathers on his white back
Building another nest
e: His brothers and sister were dozing, and "his father was preening the feathers on his white back. Only his mother was looking at him."

q: Why did the mother seagull halt motionless just opposite the young seagull with the piece of fish in her beak?
o: Because strong winds exhausted her
To tempt the starving chick into diving off the ledge out of hunger so he would be forced to fly
Because she forgot which chick was hers
To punish him before eating it herself
e: By halting just almost within reach of his beak, the wise mother used hunger as bait to force him to take the plunge.

q: After a moment of monstrous terror upon falling off the ledge, what did the young seagull feel the next moment?
o: That his wings spread outwards and the wind rushed beneath his breast and wings, lifting him smoothly
That he crashed on the rocks below
That his mother carried him on her back
That heavy rain started falling
e: The next moment he felt his wings spread outwards as wind rushed under his belly and wings—he was no longer falling headlong, he was soaring!

q: How did the seagull's family celebrate when he finally floated on the green sea?
o: They flew away silently
They ignored him for another day
They pushed him back onto the cliff
They screamed around him in praise and offered him scraps of dog-fish from their beaks
e: Around him his family screamed, praised him, and offered him scraps of dog-fish with their beaks.

q: What time was it by the narrator's watch when he was flying over France in "The Black Aeroplane"?
o: Ten at night
Twelve thirty in the afternoon
One thirty in the morning
Six in the morning
e: The narrator explicitly says: "I looked at my watch: one thirty in the morning."

q: What was the pilot dreaming about while flying over the sleeping countryside before calling Paris Control?
o: His next promotion
His holiday and being with his family in time for a good big English breakfast
A mysterious black plane
Museums in Paris
e: Under the clear starry sky, he was dreaming of his holiday and looking forward to a good big English breakfast with his family.

q: Right after Paris Control told him to turn twelve degrees west, what did the pilot do with his fuel tanks?
o: Switched over to his second and last fuel tank
Refilled the primary tank
Switched to a third reserve tank
Did not check his fuel
e: He checked the map and compass, "switched over to my second and last fuel tank, and turned the Dakota twelve degrees west towards England."

q: Inside the storm clouds, which instruments inside the Dakota stopped working?
o: Only the wing lights
Only his wristwatch
Only the landing wheels
The compass, the radio, and the other instruments were all suddenly dead
e: His compass spun wildly and died, the other instruments failed, and the radio was dead too, leaving him completely blind and lost.

q: After waving "Follow me", in which direction did the mysterious black aeroplane turn in front of the Dakota?
o: South
East
North
West
e: The text states: "He turned his aeroplane slowly to the north, in front of my Dakota, so that it would be easier for me to follow him."

q: For how long did the narrator follow the black aeroplane "like an obedient child", and how much fuel remained then?
o: For an hour; one hour of fuel left
For half an hour; only enough fuel in the last tank to fly for five or ten minutes more
For ten minutes; half a tank left
For two hours; full fuel tank
e: After half an hour, there was only enough fuel in the old Dakota's last tank to fly for five or ten minutes more, right before the runway lights appeared.

q: How did the narrator know he was safe after descending out of the storm clouds?
o: He saw two long straight lines of lights in front of him—an airport runway
Sirens rang out loudly
The black plane landed right beside him and waved
Bright daylight broke suddenly
e: Emerging from the clouds, he suddenly saw "two long straight lines of lights in front of me. It was a runway! An airport!"

q: What unresolved mystery lingers in the narrator's mind at the end of "The Black Aeroplane"?
o: Where he will eat dinner
Why Paris Control gave wrong coordinates
Why his pilot licence expired
Who the mysterious pilot was flying in the storm without lights on a plane invisible to radar
e: Learning no other plane was on radar leaves him wondering who flew that unlit black aeroplane through the storm to guide him home.

q: What humorous observation does Carolyn Wells make about the Leopard if you cry out in pain?
o: It runs away out of shame
It politely stops attacking
It will do no good to roar with pain because he will only "lep and lep again"
It climbs a tree to camouflage
e: The poet jokes: "'Twill do no good to roar with pain, / He'll only lep and lep again."

q: What does "Though to distinguish beasts of prey / A novice might nonplus" mean in "How to Tell Wild Animals"?
o: An expert hunter always gets lost
A beginner (novice) might easily get puzzled or confused (nonplussed) when trying to tell predatory animals apart
Wild beasts introduce themselves
Beginners fear small lizards
e: A "novice" is someone new to a job/skill, and "nonplus" means to be puzzled/confused—hence a beginner might struggle to distinguish predators like hyenas and crocodiles.

q: If you still have doubts after a Bear hugs you hard, what does the poet say the Bear will do?
o: He will give you "just one more caress" (another crushing hug)
He will start weeping like a crocodile
He will dive into a pond
He will roar like an Asian lion
e: Stanza 4 ends: "If you have any doubts, I guess / He'll give you just one more caress"—ironically calling a lethal squeeze a gentle "caress".

q: What is the consistent rhyme scheme of every 6-line stanza in "How to Tell Wild Animals"?
o: aabbcc
abcbab
abcabc
ababcc
e: Every 6-line stanza follows ababcc (e.g., chance/east/advance/beast/dyin'/Lion; ground/discern/round/learn/you/do).

q: What "simple rule" does Carolyn Wells give to discern the Bengal Tiger?
o: Look for black stripes on a yellow ground and "just notice if he eats you"
Check if he has no ears or wings
Check if he hugs you hard
Listen for merry laughter
e: Stanza 2 jokes: "Just notice if he eats you. / This simple rule may help you learn / The Bengal Tiger to discern."

q: Why does the poet in "The Ball Poem" say "No use to say 'O there are other balls'"?
o: Because shops were out of stock
Because that specific ball carried all his young days and cherished memories, which no new replacement can recreate
Because the boy disliked toys
Because new balls cost too much
e: The ball held "all his young days" and irreplaceable personal memories; therefore telling him other balls exist offers zero comfort.

q: What does John Berryman mean by the short statement "Money is external" in "The Ball Poem"?
o: Money can only buy outward material replacements; it cannot buy back lost emotions, memories, or internal attachment
Money is used only outside schools
The boy dropped his wallet outside
Money always stays in banks
e: Money belongs to the outer material world: it can purchase a new ball, yet it cannot restore emotional attachment or lost childhood moments.

q: What is the boy learning "well behind his desperate eyes" at the end of "The Ball Poem"?
o: How to swim in the harbour
How to sail ships
How to manufacture rubber balls
The epistemology of loss and how to stand up and accept unavoidable losses in life
e: Behind his desperate eyes, he is learning the epistemology of loss—how to endure grief and stand up again in a world where things are lost.

q: What does the phrase "In a world of possessions" imply in "The Ball Poem"?
o: Only adults are permitted to own toys
Nobody owns anything in the world
People live in a materialistic world of owning things—and therefore must inevitably face losing what they love
Everything is shared equally without loss
e: Humans naturally acquire and attach themselves to material things ("possessions"), making loss a universal human experience everyone must learn to face.

q: Where did the young seagull sleep at night when he ran back in fear from the brink of the ledge?
o: In a tall tree nest
In a little hole under the ledge
Under his mother's wing
On the sandy beach
e: The opening paragraph says he "ran away back to the little hole under the ledge where he slept at night."

q: What aerial movements were his parents, brothers, and sister performing around him once he started flying?
o: Curvetting, banking, soaring, and diving around him joyfully
Pushing him back to the rock
Hiding underwater
Sitting quietly on a cliff
e: His two brothers and sister flew around him "curvetting and banking and soaring and diving" in shared celebration.

q: What does the word "upbraiding" mean in "calling to him shrilly, upbraiding him"?
o: Praising warmly
Ignoring completely
Singing softly
Scolding or rebuking
e: Per the NCERT glossary, "upbraiding" means scolding—they scolded him to push him out of fear.

q: How did the narrator interpret the black aeroplane pilot lifting one hand and waving?
o: He thought the pilot was warning him to turn back
He thought the other pilot was lost too
He thought, "He knows that I am lost. He's trying to help me," seeing him wave "Follow me"
He thought it was an enemy fighter plane
e: Glad to see another person, the narrator saw him wave and thought: "Follow me," believing "He knows that I am lost. He's trying to help me."

q: Why did the woman in the control centre look at the narrator strangely and then laugh?
o: Because his uniform was dirty
Because he asked about another pilot when her radar clearly showed his Dakota was the ONLY aeroplane flying in that storm
Because he landed at the wrong country
Because she recognized him as an old friend
e: She laughed in disbelief at his question because in that severe storm no other planes were flying, and radar tracked only his Dakota.

q: Which animal is referred to as "a noble wild beast" in "How to Tell Wild Animals"?
o: Bengal Tiger
Asian Lion
Leopard
Bear
e: Stanza 2 explicitly introduces the Bengal Tiger as "A noble wild beast... With black stripes on a yellow ground."

q: What does "All his young days into the harbour where / His ball went" reveal about the boy's attachment to the ball?
o: He lost his fishing boat
He had bought the ball only that morning
He lived inside a ship in the harbour
The ball had been his companion throughout his childhood memories, so losing it felt like losing his innocent past
e: The ball had stayed with him for a long time; watching it sink felt like watching his joyful childhood days disappear forever.

q: Read the extract: "He failed to muster up courage to take that plunge which appeared to him so desperate." What does the phrasal verb "muster up" mean here?
o: To imitate other birds
To dive steeply into water
To hide quietly in a hole
To gather or summon courage/support
e: "Muster up" means to gather or summon inner strength or courage. The young seagull could not summon enough bravery to jump off the ledge; the other choices misread the idiom.

q: In "His First Flight", when his parents came "threatening to let him starve on his ledge", what does "threatening" convey?
o: Leaving quietly without a sound
Comforting him gently
Frightening or warning him of a harsh consequence
Sharing fresh food with him
e: As tested in JAC PYQs, "threatening" means frightening or warning someone of harm—here, his parents warned him of starvation to push him to fly.

q: Extract: "...teaching them how to skim the waves and how to dive for fish." What action does "skim the waves" describe?
o: To sink deep under the ocean water
To glide lightly just above the surface of the sea waves
To return to the cliff out of fear
To dig coastal sand with a beak
e: "Skim" means to move lightly and swiftly just over a surface. Seabirds skim right over the wave crests while hunting fish before diving.

q: Why does the mother seagull deliberately tear at a piece of fish at her feet and scrape her beak on the rock within her son's sight?
o: To heighten the starving young seagull's craving so desperation breaks his fear
To sharpen her beak for defending the nest from eagles
To show him there was plenty of leftover meat on the plateau
To signal other flocks to leave the cliff
e: Seeing his mother prepare food right across from him drove the starving bird wild with hunger, creating the emotional push needed to overcome his paralysis.

q: In "Then a monstrous terror seized him and his heart stood still", what does the idiom "his heart stood still" indicate?
o: Dancing excitedly in the sky
Falling peacefully asleep mid-air
Suffering a permanent heart ailment
Being momentarily frozen with extreme shock and fear
e: "Heart stood still" is an idiom expressing sudden, overwhelming shock or terror—felt just for a second before his wings opened naturally.

q: At the end of "His First Flight", when "His belly touched it and he sank no farther. He was floating on it", what misconception of the seagull is disproved?
o: His doubt that dog-fish were edible
His belief that his sister had shorter wings than him
His earlier fear that the vast sea would swallow and drown him
His assumption that the ledge had no sun
e: Earlier, the vast green sea terrified him because he thought he would drown. Floating effortlessly on it proves his fear was baseless.

q: When the young seagull begged "Ga, ga, ga" and his mother screamed back "derisively", what tone does "derisively" show?
o: In a tearful, apologetic whisper
In a mocking or scornful manner, rebuking his cowardice
In a sleepy, indifferent monotone
In a joyous celebratory song
e: "Derisively" means mockingly or scornfully. His mother was taunting him for still acting helpless instead of flying.

q: In "His First Flight", the narrator remarks "the precipice was sheer". What does "precipice" mean here?
o: A very steep, almost vertical rock face or cliff
A gentle sandy seashore
A grassy meadow on a plateau
A shallow stream between boulders
e: A "precipice" is a steep rock face or cliff drop. The sheer drop made the long fall beneath look terrifying to the novice bird.

q: What lesson about parenting and self-reliance does the young seagull's parents' strictness illustrate?
o: Parents should abandon children out of anger forever
Parents should permanently shelter children from all challenges
Young ones learn best when kept completely passive inside nests
Tough love and strategic pressure are sometimes essential to help children overcome fear and become independent
e: Their sternness was purposeful tough love—once the seagull took the plunge and discovered his wings, the entire family cheered and fed him.

q: Extract: "They looked like black mountains standing in front of me across the sky." Identify the poetic/literary device in "like black mountains".
o: Oxymoron
Pun
Simile
Onomatopoeia
e: Using "like" to explicitly compare huge storm clouds to towering black mountains makes this a clear Simile.

q: Extract: "I knew I could not fly up and over them, and I did not have enough fuel to fly around them to the north or south." What predicament did the pilot face?
o: His Dakota was a supersonic jet with extra tanks
Limited fuel prevented climbing over or detouring around the storm, leaving only a risky straight path or turning back
The sky above the storm was unreachable due to ATC bans
He disliked the air route to London altogether
e: Operating on limited fuel meant he could neither climb over nor detour around the storm; he had to choose between turning back to Paris or flying straight in.

q: How does the failure of both the compass and the radio inside the storm advance the plot of "The Black Aeroplane"?
o: It strips the pilot of all technological navigation, heightening suspense for the mysterious guide's arrival
It proves the pilot forgot to switch on the cockpit battery
It helped him navigate smoothly using city lights
It doubled the aeroplane's cruising speed
e: Once modern instruments fail, the narrator is completely lost in darkness, making the unexplained arrival of the unlit black plane deeply suspenseful.

q: "He knows that I am lost," I thought. "He's trying to help me." Why did the narrator draw this inference?
o: The strange plane towed the Dakota physically
The other pilot contacted him over emergency radio frequencies
Bright searchlights on the black plane illuminated London below
The other pilot waved "Follow me" and positioned his plane straight ahead of the Dakota, turning north for easy following
e: Even without radio or lights, the pilot's wave and deliberate turn northward right ahead of the Dakota clearly showed he was guiding him out.

q: What does the simile "like an obedient child" reveal about the narrator's state of mind inside the storm?
o: Overconfidence in his own instrument readings
Anger and stubborn defiance against air control
Total relief, trust, and humble dependence in a moment of helplessness
Playful carelessness mid-flight
e: Stripped of control with dead instruments and five minutes of fuel left, the experienced pilot surrendered completely to the rescuer's lead.

q: When the narrator lands safely and looks back only to find "The sky was empty", what literary effect does this sentence create?
o: Proof that the second plane had diverted back to Paris
Deep mystery, wonder, and a sense of the supernatural
Evidence that no storm clouds ever existed
Confirmation that the Dakota never left the runway
e: The sudden disappearance of the unlit plane—followed by zero radar trace—creates an enduring mystery about who or what saved him.

q: What inference can best be drawn about the narrator's character from his actions before entering the storm?
o: His eagerness to reach home for family breakfast clouded his professional judgement and made him take an unnecessary risk
He wanted to test his Dakota's crash resistance intentionally
He was a trainee unaware of basic weather hazards
He completely misunderstood Paris Control's English directions
e: Despite knowing he lacked fuel to detour, his intense longing for home and an English breakfast overruled safe aviation judgement.

q: In "Two long straight lines of lights in front of me. It was a runway!", what is a "runway"?
o: A brightly lit city highway
A narrow railway track across mountains
A wooden dock over a harbour
A paved, lit strip at an airport used by aircraft for take-off and landing
e: A runway is the marked airport strip where planes land and take off; spotting its parallel lights meant immediate rescue.

q: In "How to Tell Wild Animals", why does Carolyn Wells deliberately spell "dying" as "dyin'" and "leapt/leap" as "lept/lep"?
o: Personification
Oxymoron
Poetic licence
Simile
e: Altering conventional spelling or grammar ("dyin'" to rhyme with "Lion", "lep" for rhythm with "lept") is a textbook example of Poetic Licence.

q: In "Whose hide with spots is peppered", what does the word "peppered" convey about the Leopard's skin?
o: Seasoned with hot spices for cooking
Covered or dotted all over with dark spots like sprinkled pepper
Marked solely with long white stripes
Scorched by forest wildfires
e: Just as ground pepper scatters tiny dark specks, the leopard's hide is thickly speckled with dark rosette spots.

q: Which poetic device is prominently featured in "He'll only lep and lep again" from "How to Tell Wild Animals"?
o: Repetition and Alliteration (plus Poetic Licence)
Simile
Metaphor
Transferred Epithet
e: Repeating the coined verb "lep" creates Repetition, while the repeated /l/ sound and altered spelling showcase Alliteration and Poetic Licence.

q: In "How to Tell Wild Animals", calling a bear's fatal hug "one more caress" is an example of:
o: Apostrophe
Solemn lamentation
Simile
Irony (darkly humorous contrast)
e: Calling a bone-crushing fatal hug a gentle "caress" (loving touch) is sharp verbal Irony for comic effect.

q: Identify the sound device used in the phrase "when roaming round" in "How to Tell Wild Animals".
o: Metaphor
Onomatopoeia
Alliteration (repetition of initial /r/ sound)
Oxymoron
e: Adjacent words "roaming" and "round" begin with the same /r/ consonant sound, creating Alliteration.

q: What biological behaviour of the chameleon gives rise to the witty paradox "If there is nothing on the tree, / 'Tis the chameleon you see"?
o: Its habit of flying away as soon as humans arrive
Its ability to camouflage by changing skin colour to blend seamlessly with the tree bark or leaves
Its habit of hiding underground beneath roots
Its microscopic size invisible to human eyes
e: A true chameleon blends completely into its background through camouflage, making it look as though nothing is sitting on the branch.

q: In "A novice might nonplus", what does the verb "nonplus" mean?
o: To be confused or completely puzzled
To burst out laughing happily
To pounce bravely on wild prey
To multiply rapidly in numbers
e: "Nonplus" means to confuse or perplex someone so badly they do not know what to think—a beginner easily mixes up beasts of prey.

q: Extract: "Merrily bouncing, down the street, and then / Merrily over — there it is in the water!" Which poetic device gives the ball human-like joy ("Merrily")?
o: Pun
Oxymoron
Hyperbole
Personification

Happily
Sadly
Loudly

Alliteration (repetition of the /b/ sound in buys, ball, back)
Simile
Pun

q: In "An ultimate shaking grief fixes the boy", what does the word "fixes" mean in this context?

Simile
Oxymoron

e: It is the boy who feels desperate, not his eyes themselves; transferring the human emotion to a body part is a Transferred Epithet.

Harbour waters should be fenced off from playgrounds

q: In "His First Flight", what deeper philosophical contrast do the cramped rock ledge and the vast open sky represent?
o: Winter hibernation versus summer migration across oceans
The paralysing comfort zone of fear versus the liberating self-discovery that comes only through courageous risk
Predatory sea birds versus gentle land mammals
Ancient coastal myths versus modern city life
e: The ledge symbolizes a false, suffocating comfort zone where fear starves potential; the sky stands for freedom unlocked by taking the first leap.

q: What crucial paradox connects hunger and flight in Liam O'Flaherty's "His First Flight"?
o: The very deprivation (starvation) that seemed cruel became the exact survival force that shattered his mental block and freed his wings
Eating more fish made the bird too heavy to lift off the plateau
Even after tasting fish mid-air, he preferred staying hungry in the hole
Starvation permanently weakened his feathers during flight
e: Deprivation initially feels harsh, yet primal hunger becomes the catalyst that breaks psychological paralysis and activates his innate ability to fly.

q: What universal human insight is captured in "He forgot that he had not always been able to fly"?
o: Natural instincts erase all memories of childhood hardships
Flying at high altitude causes temporary memory loss in seabirds
Success automatically makes young ones forget their parents' support
Once self-doubt is conquered, mastery feels so natural that the past fear seems almost unreal
e: Fear looms huge only before action; once conquered, confidence flows so naturally that one forgets having ever been afraid.

q: Compare "His First Flight" and "The Black Aeroplane": what key thematic contrast exists between the two flyers?
o: The seagull relied on compasses while the pilot relied on bird instincts
Both flyers entered their journeys looking for lost fish over England
The seagull suffered from under-confidence and had to learn courage, whereas the Dakota pilot's impatience and overconfidence lured him into danger
Both protagonists failed to reach their destinations safely
e: Together the pair explores opposite poles of flying: overcoming paralyzing timidity (seagull) versus learning humility after reckless overconfidence (pilot).

q: Critics offer multiple interpretations of the mysterious black aeroplane. Which reading best captures its literary richness?
o: It was a military stealth jet sent secretly by Paris Control with broken radios
It represents either supernatural grace, a guardian presence, or the pilot's own subconscious survival instinct guiding him through panic
It was an optical illusion created by airport runway floodlights inside the clouds
It belonged to the woman at the control tower who secretly landed before him
e: Forsyth leaves the ending deliberately open-ended—inviting readers to view the black plane as divine providence, a phantom pilot, or awakened inner intuition.

q: What irony lies in the pilot thinking "I'll take the risk" right before saying "I could not see anything outside the aeroplane"?
o: He treated the storm casually for the sake of a warm breakfast, yet within seconds he was blind, instrument-less, and facing imminent death
He knew storm clouds over England always bring calm sunshine
He followed Paris Control's explicit command to fly through black clouds
Being unable to see actually improved his compass accuracy
e: Risking life and an old aircraft merely to reach breakfast on time—and instantly realizing total helplessness—creates sharp situational irony.

q: What psychological shift in the narrator is revealed by contrasting his bold decision before the storm with acting "like an obedient child" inside it?
o: Acting childishly proved his Dakota had autopilot enabled
He temporarily forgot aviation physics because of low oxygen
He secretly disliked flying solo and preferred having a co-pilot
Self-willed impatience before danger gives way to total humility and surrender when human technology fails against nature
e: His shift from defiant risk-taker to "obedient child" reveals how overwhelming danger humbles human ego when machinery fails.

q: How does the control-centre woman's puzzled laugh shape the reader's final impression of "The Black Aeroplane"?
o: It shows the airport radar machine had been turned off all night
It proves the narrator suffered a hallucination before taking off from Paris
It draws a stark line between mundane radar reality and the unexplainable miracle, locking the story in haunting ambiguity
It confirms the mysterious pilot walked out through another exit
e: Her incredulous laugh anchors the story in reality—showing how completely impossible the rescue looked on official radar—and amplifies the mystery.

q: Why is the current ending of "The Black Aeroplane" more impactful than a moralistic story where the pilot safely turned back to Paris?
o: Returning to Paris would have violated international air traffic agreements
The actual story explores human vulnerability, faith, and unexplained grace amidst folly, whereas turning back would have been a routine aviation safety memo
The actual ending serves mainly as a mechanical guide for Dakota engines
Flying back would have exposed who the woman at the radar was
e: Rather than a flat cautionary tale about fuel safety, surviving through an inexplicable guide adds depth, awe, and psychological resonance.

q: Symbolically, why might the rescuing black aeroplane have "no lights on its wings"?
o: Its unlit, shadowy form sets it apart from ordinary aircraft—suggesting a phantom, subconscious projection, or spirit-like rescuer visible only to the narrator
Storm hailstones had shattered all its wing bulbs
Its pilot switched off wing lights solely to conserve fuel
British aviation law banned aircraft lighting after 1:00 a.m.
e: Being pitch-black, unlit, and invisible on radar marks the aircraft as something beyond ordinary physical aviation—a phantom or spiritual presence.

q: What shared symbolic role do the "vast green sea" (for the seagull) and the "black storm clouds" (for the pilot) play across both flying stories?
o: Both serve merely as colourful background scenery with no conflict
Both symbolize luxurious vacation spots awaiting the protagonists
Both prove that nature always defeats every flyer
Both represent daunting, unknown obstacles that strip away complacency and demand courage or humility to cross
e: Each vast, terrifying expanse tests the protagonist at the edge of safety, forcing transformation before reaching solid ground.

q: Which literary technique drives the overarching humour of Carolyn Wells's "How to Tell Wild Animals"?
o: Presenting a serious veterinary textbook with Latin taxonomy
Giving every jungle beast long philosophical monologues
Dark humour and ironic understatement—treating fatal animal attacks in the breezy, helpful tone of a cheerful guidebook
Mourning the extinction of Asian wildlife in tragic elegy
e: Framing fatal encounters—being eaten, roared at to death, or hugged fatally—as "helpful tips" creates delightful dark humour and situational irony.

q: Why is calling the Bengal Tiger "a noble wild beast" right before "Just notice if he eats you" ironic?
o: Because Bengal Tigers are strictly herbivorous animals
The grand word "noble" (and "greets you") suggests royal courtesy, sharply clashing with the brutal reality of being devoured on the spot
Because the poet believes tigers are too timid to hunt humans
Because tigers live exclusively in freezing polar regions
e: Polite phrasing like "noble" and "greets you" collides hilariously with "notice if he eats you," sharpening the poem's comic irony.

q: What is the satirical edge in "If you have any doubts, I guess / He'll give you just one more caress"?
o: If a victim somehow survives with doubts after the first crushing hug, the bear's second deadly squeeze removes both doubt and life
The bear gently massages tired hikers in the yard
Two hugs tame a wild bear into a friendly house pet
The bear forgets its own species unless hugged twice
e: The joke hinges on verbal irony: "clearing doubts" through "one more caress" darkly implies being hugged to death.

q: How does Carolyn Wells draw upon traditional animal folklore when contrasting the Hyena and the Crocodile?
o: She insists neither creature can ever harm a human
She claims both species are affectionate vegetarians
She argues that hyenas weep softly while crocodiles laugh aloud
She playfully uses folk tropes: the hyena's cackling "merry smile" and the crocodile's proverbial false tears while devouring prey
e: Wells turns well-known idioms (laughing hyena, crocodile tears) into witty identification clues for a confused novice.

q: What is the fundamental absurdity behind the "identification rules" in "How to Tell Wild Animals"?
o: The rules work only if the animals wear printed nametags
All six animals live peacefully inside the same backyard
Every identification test proves fatal or painful to the observer, making the "useful knowledge" hilariously useless in practice
You can identify each beast safely from ten kilometres away
e: Knowing what is killing you only as it kills you renders the guide absurdly pointless—which is the central comedic joke of the poem.

q: In John Berryman's "The Ball Poem", what does the lost ball symbolize on a deeper philosophical level?
o: Merely a cheap rubber sphere worth exactly one dime
Innocence, cherished youth, and everything dear in life that we inevitably lose and cannot buy back
A sailor's navigational instrument dropped off a ship
Academic grades earned during primary schooling
e: Far more than a toy, the ball embodies childhood innocence and every irreplaceable attachment lost during human growth.

q: What vital insight into guiding children does the speaker's refusal to "intrude" or replace the ball convey?
o: Instead of shielding children from every painful loss with instant replacements, adults must let them build inner resilience and accountability
Adults should never buy toys or balls for young children
Parents should punish children whenever a toy is accidentally lost
Material gifts immediately cure deep emotional grief
e: Quickly handing out a replacement denies a child the crucial growth of coping with real loss and developing inner maturity.

q: What does "He senses first responsibility / In a world of possessions" signify about the boy's inner transformation?
o: He decides never to own any belongings ever again
He is hired to guard boats anchored along the harbour wall
He realizes his parents must always replace anything he drops
He awakens to the adult reality of caring for what one owns and bearing the consequence when things slip out of reach
e: Responsibility begins when a child realizes possessions are fragile and no outsider can erase the personal impact of losing something precious.

q: By writing the blunt sentence "Money is external", what limitation of wealth does John Berryman expose?
o: Coins cannot be used to purchase sports equipment
Currency notes are useless near coastal harbours and docks
Money acts only on the outside surface of life—buying substitutes—without touching inner grief, love, or personal memory
Wealthy individuals never suffer emotional loss
e: Calling money "external" means it remains outside the soul: it buys another object, never the emotional bond or lost past.

q: What philosophical attitude toward adulthood closes "The Ball Poem" in the phrase "knowing what every man must one day know... how to stand up"?
o: Refusing to care about anyone or anything to avoid future pain
Stoic resilience—the maturity to accept inevitable losses and rise again to face life with quiet strength
Expecting strangers to rescue every lost possession
Believing material wealth prevents all sorrow in adulthood
e: The poem ends on quiet resilience: loss happens repeatedly to everyone, and wisdom lies in standing back up and moving forward.

q: How does the syntax in "What, what is he to do? I saw it go / Merrily bouncing, down the street, and then / Merrily over — there it is in the water!" mirror the moment of loss?
o: The breathless run-on lines and sudden dash (—) mirror the swift, helpless glide of the ball until it abruptly plunges into the water
Strict classical rhyming couplets slow down the emotional pace
The lines celebrate how exciting harbour water sports are
The repetition makes the speaker sound angry at the ball
e: Enjambment and the sharp dash capture both the rapid bounce down the street and the abrupt shock when it vanishes.

q: How do both "His First Flight" and "The Ball Poem" explore the theme of growing up ("coming of age")?
o: The seagull outgrows physical fear to gain independence, while the boy outgrows childish shock to gain emotional resilience after loss
Both characters learn competitive swimming in the harbour
Both works show parents solving every difficulty immediately
Both protagonists stay trapped in fear until others rescue them
e: One portrays stepping into independence despite fear; the other depicts stepping into maturity despite heartbreak.

q: How does Frederick Forsyth use the shrinking fuel supply ("last fuel tank", "five or ten minutes") in "The Black Aeroplane"?
o: To prove Paris airport attendants forgot to refuel the Dakota
To educate readers on the fuel economy of vintage aircraft engines
As a classic ticking-clock device that escalates suspense to maximum tension right before the sudden sight of runway lights
To explain why the compass stopped turning eastward
e: Narrowing fuel down to "five or ten minutes" creates a classic ticking-clock climax just before the runway lights emerge.

q: Why does Liam O'Flaherty highlight the family's ecstatic celebration once the young seagull begins flying?
o: To show the older siblings had failed to catch any fish earlier
To prove their earlier sternness sprang from love, and that family encouragement celebrates hard-won independence
To demonstrate that seagulls can survive without ever resting
To prove the young seagull flew faster than his father permanently
e: Their immediate joyful cries and gifts of dog-fish confirm that their earlier coldness was purposeful tough love, not neglect.

q: Which human flaw triggers the entire crisis in "The Black Aeroplane"?
o: Impatient longing for personal comfort (holiday and breakfast) overriding sound safety judgement
Greed for earning double cargo fees on a night flight
Severe fear of speaking French with Paris Control
Physical exhaustion after flying for twenty straight hours
e: Letting personal impatience overrule objective danger (storm clouds plus limited fuel) is the relatable human flaw driving the crisis.

q: What cumulative effect do gentle, human-like phrases such as "greets you", "merry smiles", and "one more caress" produce in "How to Tell Wild Animals"?
o: They turn the poem into a mournful elegy for lost forests
They persuade readers that wild predators are gentle pets
They suggest the poet lacked real knowledge of Asian wildlife
They build a hilarious contrast between polite human manners and savage predation, sharpening the poem's comic tone
e: Euphemizing deadly attacks as polite greetings, smiles, and caresses creates sustained ironic contrast between civility and savagery.

q: In "The Ball Poem", how does John Berryman ultimately present the experience of "loss"?
o: As an unhealable tragedy from which nobody can recover
As a rare accident that happens only to careless children
As a painful yet indispensable teacher that awakens responsibility and builds enduring emotional strength
As a purely financial setback solved easily by pocket money
e: Berryman acknowledges the sharpness of grief while framing loss as a universal rite of passage toward maturity and resilience.

q: What critical misreading must a young reader avoid when studying Carolyn Wells's "How to Tell Wild Animals"?
o: Reading the stanzas in sequential order rather than backwards
Taking the ironic advice literally as safe wildlife instructions instead of recognizing its playful hyperbole and dark comedy
Assuming the Bengal Tiger lives on the Indian subcontinent
Thinking the chameleon has neither wings nor ears
e: Missing the tongue-in-cheek irony and treating deadly "identification" tips literally completely misunderstands the poem's comic genre.

q: Synthesizing the prose and poetry of Chapter 3 ("Two Stories about Flying", "How to Tell Wild Animals", "The Ball Poem"), what common thread unites survival and growth?
o: Genuine growth and self-awareness require confronting real fear, danger, or loss rather than hiding behind illusions or easy substitutes
Money and comfort effortlessly solve every crisis in life
External magic rescues everyone even without personal effort
Fear is permanently superior to taking thoughtful action
e: Whether conquering fear on a cliff, facing peril in storm clouds, or grieving a lost ball, maturity emerges only by confronting reality directly.
